newsitem.title: ALBANIA: Albanian election crisis talks drag on.
newsitem.headline: Albanian election crisis talks drag on.

text.p: Albanian Prime Minister Bashkim Fino haggled all day and into the night with political parties on Monday, hoping to end a row that threatens planned elections.

The June 29 elections are a vital element in bringing order back to Albania, engulfed by riots and looting in February and March after thousands of people lost their life savings in collapsed pyramid investment schemes.
But most political parties have vowed to boycott the vote, saying that current election laws favour President Sali Berisha and his former ruling Democratic Party.
As the talks continued into the evening, Fino's spokesman could not say whether they were likely to continue on Tuesday.
"There seemed to be a constructive attitude, especially in the afternoon," the spokesman said.
"They are trying and let's hope that they find a compromise," he added.

He said disagreement still centred on how many seats would be decided by proportional representation and how many by majority voting, an issue that has split the Democratic Party and the other parties for months.
Fino leads a nine-party Government of National Reconciliation, which Berisha was forced to install in March to calm the population as the rioting reached its peak.
Fino's Socialist Party, the second-largest party, wants more seats on a proportional basis to give small parties more of a chance, favouring the forming of a coalition government.
The Democrats favour more seats to be decided by majority voting, leading to the creation of a two-party system, likely to be dominated by the Democrats and the Socialists.
The talks took place under the shadow of continued violence, which is fuelled by the million or so weapons looted from state arsenals during the troubles.
Police said seven people had been killed overnight on Sunday, including two in the southern port town of Vlore who were murdered by masked gunmen at a cafe.

Frightened residents of Vlore, at the heart of the March lawlessness, refused to send their children to school although armoured vehicles of the Italian-led multinational force, which is protecting aid supplies, were patrolling the town.
German Foreign Minister Klaus Kinkel kept up constant Western pressure for a compromise as he spoke with Fino by telephone late on Sunday.
"This is in the interests of the Albanians and of the international community, which is committed to help Albania overcome the crisis," state-run news agency ATA quoted Kinkel as telling Fino.

Kinkel's warning came after statements from the European Union, Italy and the Organisation for Security and Cooperation in Europe (OSCE), which have said they may withdraw aid unless free and fair elections go ahead.
Italy, which leads the multinational force has said the troops may pull out if the elections fail.
In the last elections in 1996, the Socialists pulled out on the last day. The international community wants to avoid a repeat of that poll, which the OSCE described as deeply flawed.
